entities.name: Titus Romilius Rocus Vaticanus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Titus Romilius Rocus Vaticanus was a prominent Roman patrician politician and military commander of the early Roman Republic, whose career was deeply intertwined with the intense social and political struggles between the patrician aristocracy and the burgeoning plebeian class in the mid-5th century BCE. Serving as consul in 455 BCE alongside Gaius Veturius Cicurinus, he engaged in military campaigns against the Aequi and Volsci, securing a decisive victory and returning to Rome with significant spoils. His later, more controversial role as one of the second decemvirate in 451 BCE placed him at the heart of the monumental effort to codify Roman law, an endeavor that profoundly shaped the legal foundations of the Republic.

During his consulship, Romilius, along with his colleague, faced condemnation by the plebeian aediles and tribunes for alleged mismanagement of war spoils and for imposing a disproportionate tax on the plebeians to fund religious ceremonies. This legal challenge, which resulted in a substantial fine, highlighted the growing power of the plebeian tribunes to hold even consular magistrates accountable. His subsequent election to the second decemvirate, a powerful commission tasked with drafting the Laws of the Twelve Tables, saw him contribute to Rome's first comprehensive written legal code, a foundational document that aimed to bring transparency and equity to the judicial process, albeit initially with a patrician bias.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Titus Romilius Rocus Vaticanus's involvement in the Decemvirate directly contributed to the codification of the Laws of the Twelve Tables, a foundational legal text that shaped Roman jurisprudence for centuries. His career also exemplifies the intense class struggles and institutional development of the early Roman Republic.
